ready.title: Programme identity and purpose
ready.body:
Cyber Ready is a separate, fully online introduction to safe digital decision-making, primarily for S1 pupils.
Learners help the fictional Scottish community of Port Clyde prepare its connected community festival. A
suspicious ticket message, unsafe account settings and an overshared festival post create practical decisions
with understandable consequences. Locations include a school, library, community hall and ferry booking
desk; no knowledge of Scottish geography is assessed.

The programme develops awareness of common threats, phishing decisions, account protection, privacy and
help-seeking. It prepares pupils for safer everyday participation and offers progression towards CyberScot –
Cyber Investigator. 

WCS programme lead, school contacts and reviewer: to be confirmed.

ready.title: Access, delivery and inclusion
ready.body:
Beginners are welcome. Learners need basic browser navigation and access to a school-
managed device. S1 is the primary audience, not an entry restriction; schools judge suitability by readiness. A
short ungraded diagnostic checks navigation, reading support and the difference between private and public
information. A learner who needs support is supported rather than excluded.

All core teaching, practice, assessment and evidence submission take place in a browser. No installation,
paid licence, personal social-media account, live hacking site or real password is required. Programme
activities use fictional data and inert .example addresses. Teachers can deliver in school computer lessons or
through supervised online sessions. Fully online describes the resources and workflow; regular teacher
guidance remains part of the Cyber Ready design.

Use short screens, text equivalents for visuals, semantic headings, keyboard controls, visible focus, labelled
fields and a non-drag alternative for every sorting task. Target WCAG 2.2 AA in production, subject to audit.
Provide optional audio with transcripts, zoom/reflow, reduced motion, untimed activities, save/resume and
text or recorded-oral responses. Learners must never be required to disclose a personal experience of harm.
Equivalent oral answers are recorded against the same criteria; literacy accuracy is not a cyber assessment
criterion.

ready.title: Learning design and progression
ready.body:
Mission 1 introduces information, accounts, devices and permission. Mission 2 develops message checking
with a simulated inbox and branch feedback. Mission 3 uses a simulated settings panel; it never measures a
real password. Mission 4 uses a fictional profile and safety scenarios. Each mission has a short story briefing,

model, guided practice, independent practice, a knowledge check and a reflection. The teaching handbook
supplies exact stimuli, answers and prompts.

Award a practice badge when a mission is complete. Give feedback on how the learner checked the evidence and allow another attempt.

ready.title: Final practical assessment and decision rules
ready.body:
Use the unseen Keep Port Clyde Connected pack in the assessment handbook. The learner completes Tasks
A–E in a school-approved browser workflow. The stop–check–choose–tell card and a glossary are allowed.
Previous model answers, generative AI assistance and peer collaboration are not allowed in the final
submission. A teacher observes in class or schedules short individual online checks. Schools provide an
equivalent alternative for learners unable to join a live online session; continuous webcam recording is not
required.

All eight criteria must be met. There is no compensatory percentage or practice-score threshold. An unsafe proposed
action means the relevant criterion is not yet met, even if the learner earned practice points. The assessor
identifies the exact evidence and records met/not yet met for each criterion. Any suspected authenticity
concern triggers a supportive oral check using an equivalent scenario; it is not an automatic misconduct
finding.

Feedback identifies the unmet standard without giving the answer to a live replacement task. Offer targeted
teaching then an equivalent reassessment of unmet criteria using Version B. Retain achieved criteria where
evidence remains valid. The working proposal allows two supported reassessment opportunities, with
further attempts determined through WCS policy rather than an automatic permanent fail. Learners can
request a review through the school and WCS appeals route once confirmed. The accessible learner guide
must publish that route before live assessment.

ready.title: Evidence and teacher dashboard requirements
ready.body:
Each record needs a WCS-approved pseudonymous candidate ID, school/cohort, programme and content
version, task/criterion ID, attempt ID, response/action data, recorded support, assessment date, assessor
judgement and comment, authenticity check, IV status and release authorisation. Store a controlled name-
to-ID mapping separately. No pupil names, passwords or sensitive personal details belong in free-text
examples or demo exports.

The learner view shows missions completed, practice feedback and assessment awaiting review/met/not yet
met. The teacher view filters cohort, mission, criteria, attempts, accessibility/support needs where
appropriate, missing evidence and reassessment. It must show who changed a decision and when. Platform
completion alone is insufficient. Production dashboards need authenticated school access and WCS
oversight; the first prototype demonstrates browser-local tracking only.

ready.title: Quality and review
ready.body:
Review the instrument before use, compare assessor judgements and follow up any differences during delivery.

Record participation in the school pilot using the programme title, activity and date.

Review timings, access barriers, learner work and teacher feedback after each pilot. Record changes and assign a reviewer.

investigator.title: Purpose and separate identity
investigator.body:
Cyber Investigator develops evidence-based decisions about a straightforward cyber incident in a fictional
Scottish community. At Port Clyde's community festival, booking records appear to change after an unusual
login. Learners investigate account activity, permission settings, misleading AI-related claims and network
records. They must avoid blaming people or declaring that AI caused an incident without evidence.

Pupils can move on from Cyber Ready or enter after a readiness check covering messages, settings and a short log. Suggested audience: S2–S3 or suitably ready S1 pupils.

WCS programme lead, school contacts and reviewer: to be confirmed.

investigator.title: Fully online delivery and support
investigator.body:
All learning, synthetic evidence, analysis tools, reports and submission operate in a browser. There are no
live network probes, malware, real account access, terminal requirements or external AI accounts. A small
simulated network panel, sortable log table, evidence notebook and comparison viewer make investigation
possible on a school-managed device. Every required dataset is embedded or supplied digitally, including
text versions of visual material.

Teachers model techniques in practice, then learners plan the final investigation with minimum directive
supervision. A learner can ask for an instruction to be clarified or for an access adjustment; the teacher
records any substantive help. If the teacher supplies the inference or investigative route required by a
criterion, that criterion needs fresh independent evidence. Safeguarding and technical support remain
available throughout.

Apply the same accessible design as Cyber Ready: keyboard operation, screen-reader labels, adequate
contrast, reflow, no timer, optional transcript-supported audio and equivalent oral reporting. Avoid
diagnosing deception from faces, voices, accents, grammar or visual artefacts alone. Do not create
impersonations of real pupils or staff. Use fictional people and text-based AI provenance scenarios; no
biometric processing is needed.

and contained; it is not a professional forensic exercise or a claim of advanced attribution ability.

investigator.title: Mission structure and gamification
investigator.body:
The Incident Desk models authorised scope and evidence preservation. Signals in the Evidence teaches event
ordering, clock assumptions and comparison of hypotheses. Secure the Community Network uses a diagram
with a text equivalent and settings simulation. The Deception Studio contrasts official announcements with
unsupported AI-related claims.

Each mission includes a briefing, a worked example, practice and review. A case-file badge records completion. Use feedback to reward careful reasoning and responsible handling of evidence.

practice storyline's solution. It earns an assessor-confirmed programme result, not an automatic score-based
award.

investigator.title: Independent final assessment
investigator.body:
Use the Harbour Lights case and Version B described in the assessment handbook. Learners have a case
brief, numbered exhibits, blank plan/evidence/report fields and a glossary. They may use the supplied
browser tools, calculator and their own brief concept notes. No model reports, peer collaboration, live
internet research or generative AI assistance is permitted during the assessment. Teacher checks focus on
authenticity and scope, not directing the solution.

Accept approximately 400–700 words, a structured table with concise commentary, or an equivalent
recorded briefing of around five minutes. These are planning guides, not word-count pass rules. A learner
must satisfy all eight criteria. A strong report with missing provenance still has CI1.2 not yet met; a correct
guess without referenced reasoning does not satisfy CI2.2. Equivalent justified conclusions are accepted,
including a carefully argued inconclusive finding where it addresses all material evidence.

The assessor records criterion-level decisions, exact evidence locations, support and a short authenticity
check where needed. Feedback is criterion-specific. After targeted learning, reassess unmet criteria using a
fresh equivalent dataset. Retain valid achieved evidence. Two supported reassessments are the working
proposal; WCS policy determines further opportunities, appeals and malpractice processes. Communicate
confirmed arrangements before live assessment.

investigator.title: Evidence and teacher review
investigator.body:
Maintain versioned source exhibits, learner plan, evidence register, timeline/calculation, hypothesis
comparison, security response, claim check, final briefing and reflection. Each item is associated with
candidate, school/cohort, programme/content version, attempt, criterion, assessor and IV record. Record
judgements and changes separately from machine activity. Clicking every exhibit proves access, not analysis.

The teacher dashboard should show missing evidence, individual explanations and follow-up actions.

Sample decisions across schools and assessors and close actions after review. CyberPathways informs this proposed approach.

investigator.title: Review and approval record
investigator.body: Record the programme lead, school reviewers, instrument versions, review dates and agreed actions. Use pilot timing, pupil feedback and assessor agreement to decide what to revise.

resources.title: Delivery instructions
resources.body:
Allow 15 school periods of 50 minutes. Each contains 40 minutes of planned learning, leaving 10 minutes for logging in, transitions and packing up. The 600 learning minutes exclude those routines. Save work at each lesson boundary and resume next lesson. Timings are estimates; a pupil who needs longer can pause and resume.

Give learners the relevant mission text, stimuli and blank response fields below through the school-approved
online environment. Release teaching examples during learning; release final case exhibits only at
assessment. Teachers can edit this source and the Word copy. The first interactive build implements Cyber
Ready Mission 2; the other mission activities below are complete content blueprints and digital-ready tasks,
not yet software implementations.

Fictional .example addresses are display text, never links to visit. Never ask learners to enter a real password,
upload private messages or test a real school network. Use a neutral response when a pupil mentions a real
incident: stop the activity if needed, reassure, and follow the school's agreed reporting/safeguarding route
without recording the disclosure in the game.

Use the notional timings in the specifications. At each mission start state the learning goal; at the end ask the
learner what evidence shows their learning. Reading help, transcripts and equivalent oral responses are
available. Record support at assessment, but do not penalise an access adjustment that preserves the
outcome.

resources.title: Cyber Ready induction — lesson 1
resources.body:
Lesson 1 · Induction
15 min: Try the inbox controls · 25 min: Complete the readiness check and record any support needed

Learner briefing: “Port Clyde is putting its community festival online. Your job is to keep people, accounts and
information safe. You are allowed to pause and ask for help. All people, messages and settings in this course
are fictional.”

Teacher sequence: introduce the four mission map (5 minutes); practise keyboard navigation, saving and
resuming (10); diagnostic choices (10); agree a completion goal and support arrangements (5). Diagnostic
prompts: Is a password private? Should you investigate a suspicious real link? Who can help if a message
worries you? Expected: yes; no, use a trusted route; teacher/trusted adult/school reporting route. Diagnose
needs, do not grade.

resources.title: Cyber Ready Mission 1 — Port Clyde Goes Online — lessons 2–3
resources.body:
Lesson 2 · Port Clyde Goes Online
15 min: Identify what the festival needs to protect · 25 min: Match two risks to possible consequences

Lesson 3 · Port Clyde Goes Online
20 min: Use the four-step process on a new situation · 20 min: Explain your choice and who could help

Goal: explain what is at risk and follow a safe decision process.

Learner explainer: “An asset is something we value: a person's information, an account or a service. A threat
could harm it. A vulnerability is a weakness that makes harm easier. Permission matters: only change or test
things you have been allowed to use. Stop, check what you know, choose a safe action, and tell someone
who can help.”

Model: a public festival spreadsheet contains pupil phone numbers. Asset: private contact details.
Weakness: public access. Possible harm: unwanted contact. Action: tell the authorised organiser and ask
them to restrict access; do not copy or repost the data.

Activity 1, asset cards: festival ticket account; class register; library booking website; home address in a chat.
For each, name what should be protected. Expected: account access/tickets; personal information; service
availability and booking records; private location information. Accept equivalent plain language.

Activity 2, consequence cards: (a) shared login lets another person change a booking; (b) an update is
ignored and a known fault remains; (c) a public chat post contains a phone number. Match each to one asset
and one plausible consequence. Feedback: a concerns account/record integrity; b device/service risk; c
privacy. Avoid claims that any incident is certain.

Activity 3, decision branch: “A friend asks you to try logging into another pupil's festival account to check if it
is safe.” Choices: try once; ask for their password; decline and tell a teacher about the concern. Expected:
decline and tell; curiosity is not permission. Learner writes a two-sentence response to the friend.

Check: explain two different risks and use the four-step card on a new library booking scenario. Teacher
checks cause and consequence, not vocabulary recall. Reflection: “One safe choice I can explain is …; one
thing I will ask about is …”. Award the Community Signal practice badge on completion, with retries.

resources.title: Cyber Ready Mission 2 — The Festival Inbox — lessons 4–6
resources.body:
Lesson 4 · The Festival Inbox
15 min: Read the model ticket offer · 25 min: Trace the sender, request and checking route

Lesson 5 · The Festival Inbox
30 min: Play the four-message inbox and save your reflection · 10 min: Compare two ways of checking a message

Lesson 6 · The Festival Inbox
20 min: Handle a fresh message independently · 20 min: Explain what to do if someone has already shared a password

Goal: judge messages using evidence, independent verification and reporting.

Learner explainer: “A phishing message tries to get you to give away information, money or access. A
message can look polished and use a familiar name. A padlock says something about the connection, not
whether the sender deserves trust. You do not have to prove a message is fake before choosing a safe way
to check.”

Model message: display name Port Clyde Tickets; sender tickets@portclyde-rewards.example; link text School
portal; displayed destination https://claim-portclyde.example/login; text “Your free pass expires in ten
minutes. Enter your school password.” Show sender mismatch with the known school domain, unrelated link
destination and password/urgency request. Model response: leave the link untouched, open the school
portal using the saved school bookmark and ask the organiser using the school directory. Use the school's
report function or tell a teacher; no reporting email is sent by the simulation.

                                                                                   of authenticity.

                                      password.”                                   fraud.

                                     our band here”; QR caption destination     person or another established contact
                                     https://band-vote.example/school-login;    route. Their account could be misused.
                                     no previous discussion.                    Never scan to investigate.
P4 School cancellation               School Office; office@portclyde-            Plausible, but disruption matters: open
                                     school.example; “Bus cancelled. Use the    the known portal/check school office. A
                                     usual school portal for updates.”          genuine-looking sender is not a
                                                                                guarantee.

For each card capture classification, two observations, chosen action, independent checking route and a
brief explanation. Do not require pupils to call a message certainly malicious when the evidence supports
uncertainty. “Verify first” is a valid safe response for plausible notices. Teacher discusses why legitimate
messages also deserve safe handling.

Branch feedback: clicking a simulated suspect link never navigates or collects credentials; say “Pause. A safer
choice is to leave it and check through a route you already trust.” Sharing it to friends: “That could spread
the risk. Report privately to someone who can help.” Reporting: “Good. Include what worried you; avoid
forwarding the link around the class.” Read the feedback and try again.

Exit challenge: “You have already typed a fictional password into the suspect page.” Expected: stop; tell
teacher/IT promptly; change the affected real account only through the genuine service if this were real, and
other accounts using the same password; follow school instructions. Do not blame the person. Award Inbox
Analyst practice badge after completion, not as a formal pass.

resources.title: Cyber Ready Mission 3 — The Account Vault — lessons 7–8
resources.body:
Lesson 7 · The Account Vault
15 min: Compare fictional passphrase strategies · 25 min: Configure a practice account and explain your choices

Lesson 8 · The Account Vault
20 min: Check recovery and two-step settings · 20 min: Correct an unsafe setting and explain the difference

Goal: choose account protections and explain their purposes.

Learner explainer: “Use a long password or passphrase that is unique to each account. Three random words
is one memorable method; do not use the examples in this course as real passwords. A password manager
can help generate and store unique passwords. Two-step verification adds another check, but you still need
to be alert to deception. Recovery details should be private and kept up to date through the genuine
service.” Security teaching is informed by NCSC guidance [S3].

Simulated settings: password strategy [same short word everywhere / unique long passphrase / pupil's name
and birthday]; two-step [off/on]; recovery address visibility [public/private]; login alerts [off/on]. No free-
text password field. Select settings and explain the first three. Expected: unique long passphrase, on, private.
Alerts on is useful but not a substitute for the other controls.

Practice comparisons: “Thistle2026” is a predictable example; “the same long phrase on every account” risks
reuse; “a unique generated password in an approved manager” can be suitable. Ask learners to explain why
length alone does not solve reuse. Never score entropy or promise a password cannot be cracked.

Branch: a classmate asks for a two-step code to fix a ticket. Expected: do not share; verify through a trusted
adult/IT route. If shared already, report promptly and follow recovery instructions. Check: learner configures
fresh fictional settings and supplies one purpose per control. Badge: Account Keeper.

resources.title: Cyber Ready Mission 4 — The Digital Footprint Trail — lessons 9–10
resources.body:
Lesson 9 · The Digital Footprint Trail
15 min: Spot disclosures in the festival post · 25 min: Produce a safer version and choose its audience

Lesson 10 · The Digital Footprint Trail
25 min: Respond to a new privacy or pressure scenario · 15 min: Identify a reporting route and justify one edit

Goal: reduce unnecessary sharing and seek appropriate help.

Fictional post: “I'm Rowan, S1 at Port Clyde School. Home alone at 14 Shore Road until 8pm. Call 07000
000000. Here is my ticket QR and a photo of my friend.” The phone number is illustrative display text only.
Learner selects remove/restrict/ask permission for each disclosure.

Expected edits: remove home address and home-alone schedule; remove phone number and ticket QR;
restrict audience appropriately; ask the friend before posting their image. A private audience reduces
exposure but does not guarantee secrecy. Learner writes a replacement: “Looking forward to the festival this
weekend!” No requirement to create or edit a real social-media profile.

Digital safety branches: (a) a game contact asks for live location: decline, stop contact if needed, tell a
trusted adult; (b) a hurtful image circulates: do not reshare, support the person, report using school
procedures; (c) a prize form asks for an unnecessary birthday/address: pause and check before providing
anything. Do not ask pupils to recount real incidents.

Check: identify three unnecessary disclosures, explain one consequence and choose an appropriate help
route. Reflection contrasts “private setting” with “safe to share”. Badge: Privacy Planner.

resources.title: Cyber Ready consolidation — lesson 11
resources.body:
Lesson 11 · Consolidation
15 min: Recall the decision process · 25 min: Complete an ungraded mixed scenario

Explain assessment conditions and allow navigation practice without exposing final case answers.
This preparation is already included in the 600-minute plan.

resources.title: Cyber Ready final practical — Version A — lessons 12–14
resources.body:
Lesson 12 · Final practical
15 min: Complete task A on risk and consequences · 25 min: Complete task B on the fair message

Lesson 13 · Final practical
20 min: Complete task C on account settings · 20 min: Complete task D on the public post

Lesson 14 · Final practical
30 min: Complete task E, including the report chart and reflection · 10 min: Check and submit your evidence

Learner brief: “The Port Clyde winter fair is about to open. Review these new materials and prepare a safe
response. Use the process card. Your own decisions and explanations matter; points from practice do not
decide your result.” Suggested allocation: A 15, B 25, C 20, D 20, E 30, final check 10 minutes. Timings guide
pacing, not pass/fail.

Task A: The fair booking account uses a shared password. A public post shows a volunteer's home address.
For each, identify what is at risk and a consequence. Apply stop–check–choose–tell to one. Record: risk 1 /
consequence / risk 2 / consequence / four-step response / who can help.

Task B exhibit: display name Port Clyde School Office; actual sender office@portclyde-bonus.example;
destination https://school-ticket-check.example/login; body “Confirm your free fair ticket now. Your school
login and one-time code are needed before 3pm.” The known portal is accessed from the school bookmark
and the office number is in the school directory. Identify two distinct reasons for concern; choose what to
do, how to check independently and how to report. Explain why an authentic-looking logo or padlock does
not settle the question.

Task C: In the simulator choose a password strategy, two-step setting and recovery visibility for a new fair
account. Explain each choice. Do not type a password.

Task D: Edit a fictional post displaying a home address, evening absence schedule, public phone number and
ticket QR. Remove/restrict at least three unnecessary disclosures and explain one risk. Choose how to seek
help if another person pressures the pupil to share a location.

Task E: Submit an incident note including what happened, two relevant observations and the safe next
action. Chart as accessible table: Monday 2 suspect-message reports; Tuesday 5; Wednesday 3. Identify the
busiest day and the total. Reflect on a learning strength, improvement and next step.

resources.title: Cyber Ready assessor key and decisions
resources.body:
CR1.1: Task A needs two different threat/asset/consequence chains, e.g. shared login → unauthorised
booking changes; exposed address → unwanted contact. Mere labels without consequence are insufficient.
CR1.2: four-step response need not repeat exact wording, but must pause, examine relevant information,
choose a safe action and identify help.

CR2.1: accept sender domain mismatch, unrelated destination, request for school password/code, or
artificial deadline. Two descriptions of the deadline count as one reason. CR2.2: leave link/code request
untouched; open known portal or contact office through directory; tell teacher/use approved report
function privately. Must explain that branding/padlock does not establish trust. “Delete it” alone omits
verification/reporting.

CR3.1: select unique long passphrase strategy, enable two-step and keep recovery information private, with
a correct purpose for each. A stronger equivalent school-approved method is acceptable. CR3.2: at least
three meaningful edits; one plausible privacy/safety consequence and an appropriate help response.
Removing harmless wording does not count.

CR4.1: clear note with event, observations and next action; Tuesday and 10 total. Minor arithmetic error
means the numerical element needs reassessment, not that all communication is failed. CR4.2: a strength
tied to work, an improvement and a feasible next action. “Everything was easy” without evidence is
insufficient. Record decisions separately for each of the eight criteria.

Version B reassessment: substitute a ferry-school trip message from travel@portclyde-refund.example,
destination https://refund-confirm.example, request for school password and recovery code. Account and
privacy settings are equivalent but reordered. Chart: Thursday 4, Friday 1, Saturday 3; busiest Thursday, total
8. Use shared trip login and public travel/home-absence details for Task A. Apply the same criterion
standard. Do not simply repeat the failed question with its answer visible.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator induction — lesson 1
resources.body:
Lesson 1 · Induction
15 min: Practise distinguishing observations from inferences · 25 min: Complete the diagnostic and record support needs

Model the difference between observation, inference and allegation. “The log shows an account was used”
is an observation; “the named account holder did it” is an unsupported attribution. Agree a case goal and
scope. Diagnostic: order two time stamps, identify a private credential and name a safe reporting role.
Provide bridge learning if needed; do not assume Cyber Ready completion.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator Mission 1 — The Port Clyde Incident Desk — lessons 2–3
resources.body:
Lesson 2 · The Port Clyde Incident Desk
20 min: Define an investigation question and scope · 20 min: Record source identifiers in an evidence register

Lesson 3 · The Port Clyde Incident Desk
25 min: Plan a bounded enquiry using a fresh incident · 15 min: Review limitations and identify an escalation point

Goal: plan authorised work and preserve evidence.

Learner explainer: “An investigation answers a specific question using information you have permission to
examine. Preserve the source, reference it and put your interpretation in separate notes. A screenshot or log
can be incomplete. Record what is missing and ask the responsible person; do not access extra accounts to
fill a gap.”

Practice brief: “A library booking changed unexpectedly. Decide whether the supplied evidence supports a
mistaken edit or possible misuse.” Exhibits: M1-E1 booking A changed 14:02 by library-helper; M1-E2
volunteer message “I corrected the room number at about two”; M1-E3 scope notice “Use supplied copies
only. Ask librarian for further records.”

Learner tasks: write goal and boundaries; choose whether to start with the booking record or volunteer
message and explain; register three exhibits; distinguish source fact from note; list an unanswered question.
Blank fields: exhibit ID / source / time basis / relevant observation / limitation. Model answer: records are

consistent with an authorised correction but do not establish permission or identity; ask librarian to confirm.
Report to librarian, not classmates.

Review check: explain why modifying a source or collecting unrelated pupil messages would harm the
investigation. Badge: Case Planner.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator Mission 2 — Signals in the Evidence — lessons 4–5
resources.body:
Lesson 4 · Signals in the Evidence
20 min: Order the supplied event records · 20 min: Calculate elapsed time and check clock assumptions

Lesson 5 · Signals in the Evidence
25 min: Compare two possible explanations · 15 min: Write a conclusion identifying uncertainty

Goal: combine records, calculate time and test explanations.

Practice exhibits, all local time on one day: M2-E1 portal failed login 10:03, success 10:07 on account event-
helper; M2-E2 booking export 10:11 by event-helper; M2-E3 organiser note “I used that account from the
library at 10:05–10:20”; M2-E4 device label guest-tablet; shared device, no person identifier. Ask learners to
build a timeline, calculate success-to-export interval, compare authorised work and account misuse, and
state a limitation.

Expected: 4 minutes; authorised export is consistent with organiser note, but shared account/device
weakens attribution. A login failure is not proof of an attack. Further evidence could be an authorised export
request or organiser confirmation. If clocks differed, the timeline might need adjustment; this dataset
explicitly uses a common clock. Learners select a table or timeline and combine log with narrative evidence.
Badge: Evidence Analyst.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator Mission 3 — Secure the Community Network — lessons 6–7
resources.body:
Lesson 6 · Secure the Community Network
20 min: Read the network map and account settings · 20 min: Link two weaknesses to risks

Lesson 7 · Secure the Community Network
25 min: Prioritise two changes and identify owners · 15 min: Explain an operational trade-off

Goal: relate settings to risk and prioritise proportionate action.

Text network: Internet → managed router → staff booking laptop and public visitor Wi-Fi. Current settings:
visitors can reach booking laptop; shared organiser login; router security updates pending; offline booking
list available. No scanner or live connection is used.

Simulation choices: separate visitors from staff systems; give individual role-based organiser accounts; apply
updates via authorised IT process; turn off all festival services indefinitely; publish all passwords so helpers
can work. Learners choose two priority actions, explain their risk reduction, assign owner and name a trade-
off. Expected: isolate visitor access by IT and secure organiser accounts promptly; planned updates are also
valid with justification. Isolation may interrupt visitor services, so preserve a safe alternative. Do not claim
the settings alone prove the observed incident used that route.

Check: given a guest-only music kiosk, decide why it should not access booking records. Badge: Network
Steward.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator Mission 4 — The Deception Studio — lessons 8–9
resources.body:
Lesson 8 · The Deception Studio
20 min: Trace a festival claim to its source · 20 min: Compare the claim with a separate record

Lesson 9 · The Deception Studio
25 min: Write an evidence-based verdict · 15 min: Explain the limits of the evidence

Goal: evaluate AI-related claims through provenance and corroboration.

Exhibits: M4-E1 anonymous text post “An AI tool has cancelled every booking”; M4-E2 official library notice
“Two records were corrected; bookings remain open”; M4-E3 booking status table 48 active, 2 corrected, 0
cancelled; M4-E4 cropped chat image with no date or source. Learner records source, claim, corroboration
and limit, then drafts a calm correction for the coordinator.

Expected: blanket cancellation claim conflicts with official status evidence. The source does not establish AI
involvement or the author's intent. Cropping limits context. Verify via official status/known organiser; avoid

resharing the allegation. “Looks AI-generated” is not evidence of falsity, and a detector score cannot settle
provenance. Ask what further trustworthy information would change the conclusion. Badge: Claim Checker.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator consolidation — lesson 10
resources.body:
Lesson 10 · Consolidation
20 min: Review method and evidence references · 20 min: Practise a short briefing using a fresh case

Explain assessment conditions without supplying the final case
sequence or likely conclusion.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator independent final — Harbour Lights — lessons 11–15
resources.body:
Lesson 11 · Harbour Lights investigation
40 min: Set your scope and begin your chosen enquiry

Lesson 12 · Harbour Lights investigation
40 min: Work on your selected evidence and save an interim record

Lesson 13 · Harbour Lights investigation
40 min: Develop and test explanations in your chosen order

Lesson 14 · Harbour Lights investigation
40 min: Develop your briefing and proposed responses

Lesson 15 · Submission and feedback
20 min: Check and submit the independent case file · 20 min: Review feedback and record your next step

These are suggested checkpoints. Learners choose their investigative method and receive all exhibits together.

Learner brief: “Harbour Lights is a fictional coastal community event. At 09:20 the coordinator reports that
two ticket records changed and a message online says an AI system cancelled the event. Investigate what the
supplied evidence supports and recommend proportionate next steps. You may use only these exhibits.
Agree your goal and responsibilities with your teacher, then choose and carry out your own method.”

Provide all exhibits together, not as a leading sequence of questions. All dates are fictional 12 February 2027,
local time, synchronised to the same clock. IP addresses are documentation examples and identify network
endpoints, not people.
ID                                                      Source and original exhibit content
H1                                                      Coordinator incident note 09:20: “Records T41 and T42 now
                                                        show the wrong session. Event remains scheduled. I have not
                                                        approved an AI booking tool.”
H2                                                      Authentication extract: 08:58 helper failed login; 09:02 helper
                                                        successful login source 192.0.2.44; 09:18 helper sign-out.
                                                        Shared helper account, two-step off. No named user or device
                                                        mapping is available.
H3                                                      Booking audit: 09:06 helper changed T41 session A to B; 09:08
                                                        helper changed T42 session A to B; 09:16 coordinator corrected
                                                        T41 and T42 to A.
H4                                                      Network configuration snapshot 08:45: visitor Wi-Fi can reach
                                                        booking service; booking editing requires account login; helper
                                                        role can edit sessions; daily backup stored separately.
H5                                                      Volunteer statement recorded 09:25: “I used the shared helper
                                                        login to check arrivals shortly after nine. I do not remember
                                                        editing the sessions. Another volunteer also knows the login.”
H6                                                      Unverified public post captured 09:12: “AI cancelled Harbour
                                                        Lights. Don't attend.” The capture has no authenticated author
                                                        details. No original media or model metadata is supplied.
H7                                                      Official status notice 09:30, retrieved through known organiser
                                                        portal: “Harbour Lights is going ahead. Two booking records
                                                        were corrected. Contact the office through the published
                                                        directory if you need help.”
H8                                                      Ticket status table at 09:30: 60 active; 2 session records
                                                        corrected within those 60; 0 cancelled. Correction is not an
                                                        additional ticket category.

Required submission: an investigation goal/scope/method and role agreement; evidence register; timeline
with at least four relevant records from two source types and one elapsed-time calculation; comparison of
two explanations; proportionate security actions with owners/trade-off; provenance-based claim check;
coherent briefing and method/practice review. Learners decide how to organise these. A blank table or
headings may be supplied; no expected conclusions are included in the learner pack.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator assessor key
resources.body:
CI1.1: goal addresses record changes and claim; scope limited to supplied records; learner chooses a
coherent sequence and refers further enquiries to coordinator/IT. Agreement can be recorded in one
sentence before independent work. CI1.2: source IDs remain intact, notes are separate, and at least one
material limitation is recorded (e.g. shared account, absent device mapping or incomplete post provenance).
A hash is not required for this bounded simulation.

CI2.1: select at least four relevant events spanning at least two types, e.g. H2 login, H3 edits/correction, H6
post, H7 status. 09:02→09:08 is 6 minutes; 09:06→09:16 is 10. Accept another correct relevant interval. No
negative or invented times. CI2.2: compare accidental authorised edit and misuse of shared credentials; use
evidence for and against each. H2/H3 establish account activity, not identity; H5 is a statement, not
conclusive proof. Best-supported conclusion: two edits were made through helper and corrected; attribution
and intent remain uncertain. AI involvement is not established. Accept an alternative bounded judgement if
it addresses conflicting evidence.

CI3.1: shared helper/two-step off and visitor reachability are supported weaknesses. Network reachability
alone is not proof of the attack path. CI3.2: prioritise authorised account security/session review and
guest/staff separation with IT/coordinator owners, or an equally defensible order. Preserve relevant records
before disruptive changes; avoid deleting logs. Explain impact, e.g. temporary helper access interruption and
safe manual arrivals. Recommend ongoing individual permissions and backup checks as appropriate, but
additional recommendations do not compensate for missing required evidence.

CI4.1: H6 is unverified; H7 and H8 independently address its event-cancellation assertion. No cancellation is
supported. Neither a detector score nor lack of metadata proves who or what authored it. CI4.2: briefing
references exhibits, distinguishes observation/inference and gives practical next steps. Review names one
investigative improvement (e.g. request account/device records through IT) and one practice improvement
(e.g. individual accounts). Do not require legal-forensic terminology or a specific report length.

All eight criteria must be met. Assessors annotate evidence references rather than allocate an aggregate
pass mark. Insufficient evidence is not yet met. An unsafe recommendation, such as testing a live guest
network without permission, requires correction and fresh evidence for the relevant criterion.

resources.title: Cyber Investigator equivalent reassessment — Version B: Community Screen Night
resources.body:
Use the same five assessment checkpoints as Harbour Lights: four periods with 40 minutes of work and one with 20 minutes of submission time. Save the case file between periods.

Use the same source types and standards with a fresh case. All times use one clock on fictional 19 February
2027. B1 coordinator 15:40: two seat allocations changed, screening continues; B2 auth 15:05 failed, 15:09
successful shared-screen-helper login from 198.51.100.22, sign-out 15:30, two-step off; B3 audit 15:13 seats
S11/S12 row C→D, coordinator restores 15:25; B4 visitor network reaches seat service, editing requires
helper role; B5 volunteer states they checked seats around 15:10 but another volunteer knows login; B6
anonymous post 15:18 “AI has cancelled the film”; B7 official portal 15:50 confirms screening proceeds and
two seat records corrected; B8 40 active reservations, 2 corrected within those 40, 0 cancelled. Valid
intervals include 4 minutes login-to-edit or 12 minutes edit-to-restoration. Do not supply the key in the
learner pack. Reassess unmet criteria; verify equivalence through IV before use.

resources.title: Feedback and marking templates
resources.body:
Assessment record fields: candidate ID; programme/version; school/cohort; attempt/version A or B;
assessment date; access arrangements; permitted support; authenticity evidence; assessor/date; criterion
ID; evidence reference; met/not yet met; rationale; feedback; reassessment action/date; IV outcome and
release status.

Example borderline record: “CI2.2 not yet met. Timeline is accurate, but report concludes the volunteer
caused the incident without considering shared access in H5. New evidence is required comparing the two
explanations and stating a justified limit.” Do not copy a completed model conclusion into a pupil's
reassessment response.

Learner review template: “A choice I can now explain …; evidence from my work …; something I still need to
improve …; my next action …”. Programme feedback/review time is 30 minutes in each learning-hour plan.
Assessment reflection can contribute evidence where it is authentic and recorded.

resources.title: Security reference notes
resources.body:
[S3] NCSC, Using online services safely: securing your users' accounts.
https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/using-online-services-safely/securing-your-users-accounts ; phishing
guidance https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams ; response advice
https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams/what-to-do . Accessed 20 November 2026. School
reporting instructions and current technical advice must be checked before live delivery. All story material
and exhibits in this handbook are original fictional teaching content.

quality.title: Design principles and responsibilities
quality.body:
Use the CyberPathways approach as a starting point: trace decisions to evidence, review materials before use, compare assessor decisions and close corrective actions.

The programme lead coordinates versions and schools. Teachers record observations, assessors explain decisions, an independent verifier checks the sample, and WCS Quality confirms local arrangements.

Named appointments, deputies and WCS policy/form references must be entered in the approval record
before operational delivery. A programme lead cannot self-authorise all stages without an independent
verification and release mechanism.

quality.title: Approval and release gates
quality.body:
Design review: check mission instructions, examples and answer guidance.
Pilot readiness: agree school contacts, device checks, support arrangements and dates.
Pre-delivery review: check assessment tasks and record corrections.

After testing, review feedback, resolve issues, record a go/revise/stop decision for each programme and confirm who will check the changes.

quality.title: Pre-delivery internal verification
quality.body:
The verifier reviews all outcomes and criteria against assessment tasks, learner instructions and keys. Check
that Cyber Ready includes supported decision stages and practical settings, and Cyber Investigator requires
an independently chosen process and combined evidence. Check accessibility alternatives, non-
compensatory decisions, data minimisation, authenticity, AI rules and equivalent reassessment. Test every
numerical key and whether an alternative reasoned conclusion could satisfy the standard.

Record: instrument/version; reviewer/date; criteria checked; validity/fairness/reliability findings; mandatory
corrections; owner/due date; revised version; closure evidence; release decision/date. Use the WCS-
approved instrument once Quality identifies it; this document's field set is a proposed content model, not a
replacement form automatically authorised by WCS.

quality.title: Standardisation before, during and after assessment
quality.body:
Before pilot: 60-minute online meeting using one clear achievement, one clear not-yet-met and two
borderline responses for each programme. Assessors judge independently first, compare criterion decisions
and record agreed examples and reasons. Cover guided versus independent work, acceptable oral evidence,
legitimate uncertainty in phishing and unsupported attribution in investigation. Calibration examples are
staff-only.

During pilot: 30-minute midpoint clinic on anonymised cases. Check whether schools are accepting
practice completion as achievement or supplying final inferences. Record disagreements and revise guidance
prospectively with version control. Where guidance was wrong, identify and review affected prior decisions
fairly.

After pilot: 60-minute review of agreement, appeals, learning time, access issues and school variation.
Produce a change log and revised exemplars. Record school/assessor attendance and follow-up for anyone
absent. Standards must not change silently within a cohort.

quality.title: Proposed sampling plan
quality.body:
For the small pilot, pre-check every instrument and sample each assessor's first five completed cases (or all if
fewer). Include at least one not-yet-met/reassessment and an access-adjusted case where available. Then
sample at least 20% of remaining assessed cases per assessor, rounded up, deliberately covering different
schools, criteria, achievement decisions and response formats. If no case in a category exists, record that fact
rather than invent one. These are proposed pilot sampling rules for WCS agreement, not claimed WCS
policy.

Expand to all affected decisions for a criterion where a material judgement error is found; restandardise,
correct records and resample before release. Risk flags include a new assessor, revised task, unusually

uniform answers, high reassessment rate, missing evidence, unexplained school variation or technical data
loss. Sampling during delivery must give time for correction before final review.

Sample record: cohort/assessor; population and sample size; selection rationale;
candidate/attempt/criterion; assessor decision; verifier decision and rationale; action owner/due date;
corrected evidence; follow-up date; closure. A sampled record is not “verified” until any required action is
closed.

quality.title: Authenticity, adjustments and learner rights
quality.body:
Use supervised in-school assessment or scheduled online checks with short individual explanations. No
continuous camera surveillance or automated facial/voice checks are required. Record the candidate's
explanation and task-specific understanding; avoid publishing pupil recordings. Use equivalent oral evidence,
readers/scribes, extra time and assistive technology where they preserve cyber decision-making and
required autonomy. Record exactly what the adult did.

The school explains permitted resources and AI use before assessment. Suspected copied/generated work
prompts an evidence-based review and an accessible opportunity to demonstrate the learning. Confirm WCS
appeal/review contacts, timescales and malpractice process before live delivery. Provide the learner with
decisions, reasons and how to ask for a review; do not invent a fixed institutional deadline in these
proposals.

quality.title: Evidence management and production architecture
quality.body:
Use a fictional ID in the demo. Capture the task version, learner response, exhibits, attempt, support and teacher judgement. Keep practice events separate from reviewed assessment decisions. Record who checked each decision and any follow-up.

Production requires school-approved authentication, role and cohort restrictions enforced on the server,
encrypted transport/storage, backup/restore testing, audit logging and a controlled export route. Browser-
local data and editable JSON are not verified assessment evidence. Do not store secrets or access tokens in
exported learner work. Confirm hosting/data location, lawful basis, controller/processor responsibilities,
privacy notice, retention/deletion schedule and any necessary impact assessment with WCS and schools. Do
not assume parental consent is the universal legal basis.

The prototype stores a pseudonymous ID, actions and text locally, without a server. It has a teacher
demonstration view available to anyone using the page; that is not authentication. Use fictional records only.
Clear local progress on shared devices after exporting required demonstration data. Production school data
must wait for the approved platform and agreements.

quality.title: Recording pilot participation
quality.body:
Record the programme, activity tested, date, number of participants and outstanding actions. Use anonymous observations for pilot reporting.

Ask the school contact to check the session summary. Assign actions and agree a follow-up date.

quality.title: School pilot design
quality.body:
Pilot in two stages. Stage 1 tests the phishing prototype with 12–18 pupils across two schools, including
keyboard/assistive-technology users where practicable. Use fictional IDs and no live pupil evidence.
Stage 2, after readiness and instrument verification, trials the complete digital-ready materials with four
schools: approximately 12–15 learners per school per programme where timetabling permits (48–60 per
programme). Cohorts can differ; do not require every pupil to do both programmes. Include urban/rural
contexts, differing connectivity and a mix of cyber experience without claiming statistical representativeness.

Proposed planning window: January–March 2027, subject to school and WCS agreement. Complete readiness and staff calibration before lesson 1. Allow 15 school periods per programme. At two periods per week, allow eight teaching weeks. Complete IV and the pilot review after lesson 15. Do not run Stage 2 final assessment on the
first local-only prototype.

Recruit schools through WCS-approved contacts; provide information for schools and families, support
contacts and withdrawal arrangements. Record reasons for non-completion without forcing sensitive
disclosures. No emails or invitations have been sent as part of this development.

quality.title: Pilot instruments
quality.body:
Learner pulse after each mission: “I knew what to do” (1–5); “I could use the controls” (1–5); “The feedback
helped me understand” (1–5); optional barrier comment without personal information. Final prompts:
explain one safe action on a fresh message; describe a point where support helped; name anything
confusing. Do not use confidence ratings as evidence of competence.

Teacher log per session: programme/mission; start/finish; active learning minutes excluding breaks, outages
and unrelated tasks; completion; support type/duration; access barrier; misconception; intervention;

resource version. Per learner, separate normal learning time, assessment time, access extensions and
reassessment. Report median/range and why outliers occurred; review whether successful learning
realistically fits 10 hours.

Assessor comparison form: candidate ID; criterion; judgement A; judgement B; evidence reference; reason
for disagreement; resolution; effect on other records. Double-mark at least ten varied submissions per
programme across schools if available. Report criterion-level agreement, not merely identical overall pass
rates.

quality.title: Pilot decision criteria and evaluation
quality.body:
Measure                             Proposed readiness threshold                  Action if missed
Safety/access                       No unresolved critical safety or access       Stop affected activity, fix and retest with
                                    blocker; required tasks keyboard-usable       users
                                    with supported alternatives
Evidence integrity                  All required criteria can be evidenced,       Hold assessment/release until corrected
                                    exported/submitted and traced to
                                    version/attempt
Marking consistency                 At least 90% criterion agreement in           Recalibrate; revise ambiguous
                                    double-marked sample, plus resolution         criteria/tasks; resample
                                    of every material disagreement
Learning time                       Typical successful learners broadly fit the   Review scope/support and notional-hour
                                    10-hour design; investigate median            rationale; revise the timing estimate
                                    outside 8–12 hours
Engagement                          At least 80% of starters complete             Revise accessibility, pacing and support
                                    planned pilot learning; examine barriers      before scaling
                                    behind withdrawal
Understanding                       Assessed evidence demonstrates criteria       Revise activities and authenticity checks
                                    rather than answer recall or point
                                    accumulation

These are proposed pilot thresholds. Report sample size and missing data; a small pilot
cannot prove national effectiveness. Record go/revise/stop separately for each programme and for platform
readiness. Record the reasons for each pilot decision.

quality.title: Risks, resources and change control
quality.body:
Main risks: 10-hour scope too broad (trim optional content and recheck timings); reading demand
obscures cyber ability (plain language/audio/equivalent evidence); school restrictions block delivery (device
check and approved hosting); badges mistaken for qualifications (separate status and wording); teacher
prompting reduces independence (calibration/support logs); evidence loss or inappropriate access
(production controls and tested exports); overconfident AI attribution (counterexamples and rubric limits).

Confirm staff time for authoring, user testing, accessibility checks, school coordination, assessment review and technical support.

Change log fields: version/date; affected programme/task; reason; outcome/level/hours impact;
accessibility/security impact; reviewer; approval; deployment date; schools informed; previous cohort
treatment. Freeze assessment versions for each cohort. Escalate substantive changes through WCS and the
programme review process before changing a live task.

quality.title: Approval record to complete
quality.body: Complete the programme lead, school coordinator, assessor, independent reviewer, pilot date, approved platform, retention period, review contact and next review date.
